sections.h2: Which city office issues an Ann Arbor tax bill?
sections.html:
Ann Arbor collects its own property tax through the Treasury unit, and the city's Assessor sets the values behind each bill. Once real property tax stays unpaid past winter, the account moves to Washtenaw County.

The city's Assessing page reports that over half of Ann Arbor's revenue comes from property tax, so assessments draw close scrutiny. A bill is a combined figure: the city levy, plus the county, the schools and other taxing units, each setting its own millage.

A separate administration fee also appears. State law lets the city add up to 1 percent of the tax, and the money offsets the work of defending assessments and collecting for every taxing unit.

sections.h2: What dates matter on the Ann Arbor tax calendar?
sections.html:
Two bills arrive each year: summer tax is billed July 1 and winter tax December 1, with the last penalty-free days at the end of those months. County operating tax rides on the summer bill, and the voted county millages ride on the winter one.

Missing the winter deadline starts a short countdown. Real property tax still unpaid on February 28 is passed to the Washtenaw County Treasurer, and extra penalties and interest begin March 1. The city's online record stops at that handoff, so confirm with the county whether a late balance has been paid.

sections.h2: How are Ann Arbor property taxes calculated?
sections.html:
Take the taxable value, divide by 1,000, multiply by the millage rate, then multiply by 1.01 for the fee. Taxable value often trails assessed value because Proposal A, passed by Michigan voters in 1994, ties its yearly growth to the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, with additions counted separately. Assessed value itself targets half of market value.

The city's estimator page shows annual millage totals of 52.8802 for principal residences and 68.8196 for other property. Run purely as arithmetic, a $200,000 taxable value at the first total comes to $10,681.80 with the fee included. Rates move from year to year, and your parcel's real bill follows the units that cover it.

Your taxable value is printed on the annual bill and on the assessment notice, which the city mails around the first week of March. The online property record card holds the figures behind both.

sections.h2: Why does an Ann Arbor tax bill jump after a sale?
sections.html:
Following a sale or transfer, the next tax year's taxable value is set equal to the assessed value, the half-of-market figure. Ann Arbor calls that uncapping. The yearly limit then applies again until ownership changes once more.

That rule is why a buyer's first full bill can top the one you paid. A long-held house may carry a taxable value well under its assessed value, and the buyer begins without that cushion. With homes valued at a median of $453,400, the difference can be sizable.

The Assessor's Office, on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, takes the Property Transfer Affidavit, the Principal Residence Exemption affidavit and the request to rescind that exemption. Hand them in, submit them on the online forms page or mail them. Ask questions at 734.794.6530 or assessor@a2gov.org.

sections.h2: How does a homeowner challenge an Ann Arbor assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the city Board of Review, which sits four days beginning the Monday of March's third week. You appear by appointment, and the Assessor hands out the appeal forms. Board members are appointed citizens, approved by council, and do not work for the city.

The case that works shows assessed value running past 50 percent of true cash value. Objecting that taxes keep climbing does not count, the city explains, because taxable value may rise yearly by inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower. Helpful evidence includes comparable nearby sales, mistakes on your record card and a repair estimate for something like a leaking basement.

  • A homeowner has to protest at the local board before taking a case to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • The Tribunal filing date is July 31 for homes, and May 31 for commercial and industrial real property and business personal property.
  • The board mails its decision some weeks after it adjourns, along with the next appeal steps.

sections.h2: Is a deferment available, and who handles a balance that went delinquent?
sections.html:
Certain owners can put off the summer bill: senior citizens, people with qualifying disabilities or blindness, and eligible servicepersons, veterans and their surviving spouses. A summer deferment carries a $40,000 household income cap. Pick up the application at the Customer Service Center, 301 E. Huron St., or find it at washtenaw.org, and file it with the treasurer by September 15.

Real property balances that moved to the county are handled by the Washtenaw County Treasurer at 734.222.6600 or taxes@washtenaw.org. Overdue personal property tax stays with the city, and 734.994.2833 gives the amount.

If you plan to sell with a bill outstanding, request the figures before you list. The closing agent pays what is owed from your proceeds.

sections.h2: What does an Ann Arbor seller need to know about the city?
sections.html:
Two land speculators founded Ann Arbor in 1824 and named it for their wives, both called Ann, and the bur oaks on the site. The town became the Washtenaw County seat in 1827, a village in 1833 and a city in 1851. The University of Michigan took root there in 1837, and the two grew up together.

The Huron River winds through town, and the Tree Town nickname rests on more than 50,000 street trees. Three freeways ring the city: I-94 on the south and west, US 23 on the east and M-14 on the north. Ann Arbor Public Schools runs the public high schools, among them Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community. The university alone employs about 30,000 workers, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center.

  • Estimated 2025 population: 122,233, down 1.3 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Owners hold 45.5 percent of 50,499 households, which makes renters the majority.
  • Typical home value $453,400, typical gross rent $1,649.
  • Household income at the midpoint: $82,212; adults with a four-year degree or more: 77.9 percent.
  • Monthly owner costs at the midpoint: $2,436 with a mortgage, $1,036 without.

Renters fill more than half of Ann Arbor's homes, so some sellers are landlords or heirs with an older house. When repairs stand in the way of a conventional sale, a buyer who takes the property as-is can close without them.

faqs.q: What is the due date for Ann Arbor summer tax?
faqs.a: July 31, with payments accepted from July 1. Winter tax runs on the same pattern, opening December 1 and closing December 31.

faqs.q: Where can I pay my Ann Arbor tax face to face?
faqs.a: Use the Customer Service and Payment Center inside Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., open weekdays 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. A drive-up drop box at East Ann Street and North Fifth Avenue stays open around the clock.

faqs.q: Does selling change an Ann Arbor taxable value?
faqs.a: Yes, for the buyer. The year after a transfer, taxable value is reset to the assessed value, a step the city calls uncapping.

faqs.q: When must an Ann Arbor homeowner file with the Michigan Tax Tribunal?
faqs.a: By July 31, after first protesting at the March Board of Review. Commercial and industrial real property and business personal property must file by May 31.

faqs.q: Who collects Ann Arbor real property tax that is still unpaid in March?
faqs.a: The Washtenaw County Treasurer, at 734.222.6600, takes real property tax not received by February 28. Delinquent personal property tax stays with the city.
